1.meaning: A name for the Day of Judgement: 'the Striking Calamity' — the catastrophe that strikes, knocks, and crashes down upon all creation with a deafening, terrifying force. The word pictures a sudden, violent blow that shatters the normal order of the world, which is why it is also rendered 'the Striking Disaster.'

parts.en: striking / clattering one (active participle, pattern fāʿil: the one that strikes); the stem ends at the ʿayn and carries no trailing vowel of its own
feminine ending: -a is the connecting vowel (fatḥa) carried on the tā marbūṭa, -t is the feminine marker, and -u is the nominative case ending

1.grammar: Built on the active-participle pattern fāʿil (here qāriʿ), which names the doer of an action — 'the one who/that which strikes.' Adding the feminine tā marbūṭa gives the feminine form qāriʿah. The final vowel is -u, the nominative case, marking it as the subject/topic standing on its own as an exclamatory title: 'The Striking Calamity!' The 'al-' makes it specific and definite — not any calamity, but THE Calamity.
1.root: ق-ر-ع (q-r-ʿ) — to strike, knock, or beat with a sudden crashing sound

1.meaning: An interrogative word meaning "What?" Here it is not a simple request for information but a rhetorical, awe-inducing question — "What IS this Striking Calamity?" — used to magnify the event's terror and signal that it is beyond ordinary comprehension.
1.grammar: An indeclinable interrogative particle/noun — it has no case ending that changes; the long final -ā is fixed. Functioning as the subject (mubtadaʾ) of the nominal sentence, it sets up the question whose answer is the following word. Its force is rhetorical: it expresses astonishment and dread rather than seeking a literal definition.

2.meaning: The Striking Calamity — a name for the Day of Resurrection. It is an active participle from a verb meaning to strike, knock, or pound violently, so it pictures a catastrophe that hammers and crashes upon the hearts and ears of all creation; the definite article "the" marks it as that one specific, well-known Day.
2.grammar: Definite (al- = "the") active participle in the feminine singular. The stem is the fāʿil pattern qāriʿ ("the one that strikes"), to which the feminine tā' marbūṭa (ة) is attached with its connecting vowel -a-, and the final -u marks the nominative case. The nominative here makes the word the predicate (khabar) answering the question — "[What is] the Striking Calamity." (The small pause mark after it is recitation notation, not part of the word.)
2.root: ق-ر-ع (q-r-ʿ) — to strike, knock, pound, beat

1.meaning: "And what..." — an opening conjunction joined to an interrogative pronoun. The wa- ("and") links this verse to the one before it, while mā ("what") here is not a simple question seeking information but a rhetorical device expressing awe and magnification: it builds suspense about the overwhelming nature of the Striking Calamity.
1.grammar: Two pieces joined together. The prefix wa- is the connector "and." The word mā is an interrogative "what," but used rhetorically to overwhelm rather than to ask. It is indeclinable (its ending never changes), so there is no case vowel to interpret here; it functions as the subject of the question that follows. The long final -ā simply belongs to the word itself.

2.meaning: "...has made you realize / could ever make you grasp" — a past-tense verb meaning to cause someone to know or fully comprehend something. Paired with the negative-rhetorical "what" before it, the sense is: nothing could have made you truly comprehend, on your own, the magnitude of this Day; only revelation can disclose it.
2.grammar: This is Form IV (the a-...- causative pattern), which turns the root sense "to know/perceive" into "to MAKE someone know." It is a past-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular ("he/it made..."), with the implied doer being the matter itself. The attached -ka is the object pronoun "you," addressed to a single male (the Prophet, peace be upon him, and through him every listener). So the whole word = "it made you realize."
2.root: د-ر-ي (d-r-y) — to know, to perceive, to be aware

3.meaning: "what (is)..." — an interrogative pronoun introducing the actual question being magnified: "what is the Striking Calamity?" It opens a noun-sentence whose answer is deliberately withheld and built up, deepening the sense of dread and grandeur.
3.grammar: A standalone interrogative "what," beginning an embedded question ("what [is] the Qāriʿah?"). It is indeclinable, so its ending never changes and carries no case vowel to interpret; grammatically it stands as the subject (mubtada, "what"), with the following noun as the predicate. The short final -ā is part of the word, not a case ending.

4.meaning: The Striking Calamity — a title for the Day of Resurrection. The word names a sudden, crushing blow that strikes hearts with terror; it is one of the names of the Last Day (alongside al-Ḥāqqah, aṣ-Ṣākhkhah, and others), evoking a catastrophe that pounds and overwhelms all creation.
4.grammar: Three pieces: the prefix al- ("the"), the noun qāriʿah, and the final vowel -u. The noun is an active participle on the fāʿil pattern (فَاعِل, "the one that strikes/pounds"), here in its feminine form on the fāʿilah pattern (فَاعِلَة). The final -u marks nominative case. In the sentence "mā al-qāriʿatu" ("what is the Striking Calamity?"), mā is the subject (mubtada) and al-qāriʿatu is the predicate (khabar) — so this word is the predicate, not the subject, and the nominative case is what a predicate of a noun-sentence takes.
4.root: ق-ر-ع (q-r-ʿ) — to strike, knock, pound, beat down

1.meaning: On the Day — pointing to the great Day of Resurrection. The word names a specific day and sets the time-frame for everything that follows: this is when mankind will be in the state described.
1.grammar: A noun fixed in the -a ending (accusative). The -a marks it as an adverb of time, 'on the Day…', tying the scene to a definite moment. Because it stands before the verb 'yakūnu' it functions as 'on the Day when (people will be)…'.
1.root: ي-و-م (y-w-m) — day, a defined period of time

2.meaning: (They) will be / it comes to pass — describing an ongoing future state rather than a single act. It introduces what mankind will become on that Day.
2.grammar: Present/future verb, 3rd-person masculine singular ('he/it will be'). The ya- prefix marks the 'he/it' subject; the final -u ending shows the verb is in its plain indicative form (an ongoing, unfolding state, not a command). Though singular in form, it agrees with the collective noun 'mankind' that follows.
2.root: ك-و-ن (k-w-n) — to be, to come into existence

3.meaning: Mankind — humankind as a whole, all people gathered together. This is the subject of 'will be': it is humanity that will be scattered like moths.
3.grammar: A definite noun, 'the people'. The prefix al- ('the') makes it definite and general — humankind as a class. The final -u ending is nominative, marking it as the doer/subject of the verb 'yakūnu' ('mankind will be…'). Nūn is a sun letter, so the 'l' of al- assimilates into it and the nūn is doubled: it is pronounced an-nāsu.
3.root: ء-ن-س (ʾ-n-s) — humans, sociable beings (from uns/ins); a minority view derives it from ن-و-س (n-w-s), to sway/move

4.meaning: Like moths — the small insects that flit and swarm chaotically around a flame. The image captures how people will mill about in confusion and terror, weak and aimless, drawn helplessly in every direction.
4.grammar: The prefix ka- means 'like / as', forming a simile. It is a preposition, so the noun after it takes the -i ending (genitive) — hence farāsh-i. 'Farāsh' is a collective noun ('moths' as a swarm). Fā is a moon (lunar) letter, so the 'l' of al- does not assimilate and stays fully pronounced: kal-farāshi.
4.root: ف-ر-ش (f-r-sh) — to spread out; (here) moths that spread and scatter

5.meaning: Scattered about — strewn and dispersed in disorder, flung in all directions with no pattern. It deepens the picture of the moths (and so of mankind) as thrown about and bewildered.
5.grammar: A passive participle ('having been scattered'), the maf'ūl pattern ma-…-ū- meaning something acted upon — i.e. moths that have been strewn about by an outside force. It describes the preceding 'moths', so it matches them: definite (al-) and ending in -i (genitive) to agree with 'farāshi'. The passive form stresses that the scattering is done to them, not by them.
5.root: ب-ث-ث (b-th-th) — to scatter, spread, disperse widely

1.meaning: And the mountains will be / become - a verb describing the transformation that will overtake the mighty mountains on the Day of Judgement. The 'and' joins this scene to the preceding image of people scattering like moths; the verb itself points to an ongoing, unfolding state ('will be / will keep becoming').
1.grammar: Present-tense verb 'to be/become' (root k-w-n). The ta- prefix marks a 3rd-person feminine singular subject ('it [she] will be'), which agrees with the feminine noun 'the mountains' that follows. The final -u ending is the indicative mood: it signals a plain, ongoing statement of fact ('will be'), not a command or a negated/subjunctive form. Joined to the previous verse by the prefix wa- ('and').
1.root: ك-و-ن (k-w-n) — being, coming into existence, becoming

2.meaning: The mountains - the towering, seemingly permanent peaks of the earth, here singled out as the very symbol of solidity and immovability, precisely so that their coming undoing can show that nothing in creation is truly stable before Allah.
2.grammar: A definite plural noun, 'the mountains' (singular jabal). The al- prefix is 'the'. This is the doer/subject (fāʿil) of the verb 'will be', and its final -u ending is the nominative case, which is the marker Arabic puts on the subject of a sentence — it tells you the mountains are the ones doing/undergoing the action.
2.root: ج-ب-ل (j-b-l) — mountain; firmness, that which is firmly fixed

3.meaning: Like tufts of wool - comparing the mountains to dyed, soft wool. The word ʿihn specifically means wool that has colour, evoking something once solid now reduced to light, drifting fluff that the wind can toss about.
3.grammar: The prefix ka- means 'like / as', forming a simile. Because ka- is a particle that governs the genitive, the noun after it takes the -i ending (genitive case) — that final -i is exactly what the 'like' attaches to, marking 'wool' as the thing being compared to. al- is 'the'.

4.meaning: Carded / fluffed-out - describing the wool as teased apart and scattered into loose, weightless fibres. Together with the previous word the image is of mountains turned into wisps of fluffed wool, drifting and dispersing — utterly stripped of their former mass and might.
4.grammar: A passive participle (something that has had an action done to it — here 'wool that has been carded/fluffed'). It is an adjective describing 'wool', so it copies that word's grammar: the al- ('the') and the final -i (genitive case) match 'wool', showing the two words belong together as 'the carded wool'. It follows the maf'ūl pattern (manfūsh), the standard Form I passive-participle shape that conveys 'having been fluffed/carded'.
4.root: ن-ف-ش (n-f-sh) — to card, tease apart and fluff up wool

1.meaning: A two-part connector opening the verse: 'so then, as for...'. The fa- signals a consequence or transition flowing from the scene just described (the Day of Judgement), and ammā sets up a 'as for / whatever the case of...' clause that will be answered later by its matching 'then' (the fa- on the reply in the next verse). Together they single out one category of people for comment.

parts.en: as for / whatever the case of

1.grammar: This is a single written word, فَاَمَّا, made of an inseparable prefix fa- attached to the particle ammā; the two are shown separately only to display the meaning, not because they are separate tokens in the text. Because both pieces are particles, there is no case-ending to read. The prefixed fa- ties this verse to what came before ('so, in light of that...'). ammā is a detailing/conditional particle meaning 'as for...'; it opens a clause whose answer must begin with fa- ('then...'), which arrives on the reply clause in the following verse. It does not change the words after it grammatically; it only frames them.

2.meaning: A relative/conditional word here meaning 'the one who / whoever'. It refers to a person (used for people, not things) and introduces the description that follows — 'whoever's scales turn out heavy'. It functions as the subject being talked about in this 'as for...' clause.
2.grammar: An indeclinable word: it is built on a fixed ending (sukūn on the n) and never changes its form for case, so there is no vowel to interpret. It works as a conditional/relative noun standing for a person, and the verb that follows (thaqulat) describes that person.

3.meaning: 'Became heavy / weighed heavy.' Describes the scales tipping with weight — here the weight of good deeds — so that the pans come down heavily. A completed, past-tense action used vividly for the future Day of Judgement.
3.grammar: A past-tense (perfect) verb. The final -at is the 3rd-person feminine singular marker ('she/it did'). It is feminine singular, not plural: the subject that follows, mawāzīn ('scales'), is a non-human broken plural, and in Arabic such plurals take feminine singular verb agreement. So although 'scales' is plural in sense, the verb is singular and the phrase means 'his scales (taken as a whole) became heavy,' not 'they became heavy.' Form I (the plain, basic verb pattern) carries the simple meaning 'to be/become heavy.'

4.meaning: 'His scales / his balances' — the weighing-scales on which a person's deeds are measured on the Day of Judgement. The plural suggests the full set of weighings or the totality of what is weighed; the attached 'his' ties these scales to the individual person referred to by 'whoever.'
4.grammar: A plural noun (singular mīzān, 'a scale/balance') carrying the -u ending, which is the nominative case: it marks this word as the subject — the thing that 'weighed heavy.' The attached -hu means 'his,' linking the scales to the person; here it is pronounced -hū (long) because it follows a vowel. So the phrase reads 'his scales weighed heavy.'

1.meaning: "Then he…" — this introduces the happy outcome for the person whose good deeds outweighed the bad. The opening fa- is a connector meaning "then/so/and so," tying this result back to the previous verse's condition ("as for the one whose scales are heavy…"). The huwa is the standalone pronoun "he," which here also adds emphasis: "he, indeed, is the one who…"
1.grammar: Two pieces joined together. The prefix fa- is a connective particle linking this clause to the prior verse as its consequence ("then/so"). huwa is an independent subject pronoun, "he," standing as the subject of the sentence; placing this separate pronoun first gives gentle emphasis ("he is the one who…"). It carries no case ending of its own — independent pronouns in Arabic are fixed in form.

2.meaning: "in" — a simple preposition placing the person inside or within something. Here it sets up where he will be: "in a life…," i.e. immersed in and surrounded by that condition of living.
2.grammar: A preposition (a small linking word). Its job is to put the noun that follows into the genitive case — which is why the next word, ʿīshatin, takes an -i (kasra) ending. fī itself does not change form; it simply governs what comes after it.

3.meaning: "a life" — not merely being alive, but a whole mode or manner of living, a state of existence and the lifestyle that goes with it. In this verse it is the blissful life of Paradise: the entire way the blessed will live, contented and at ease.
3.grammar: A feminine noun. The final -in (written as tanwīn, the doubled kasra) does two things at once: the -i shows the genitive case, required because it follows the preposition fī; and the -n (nunation) marks it as indefinite — "a life" rather than "the life." So the ending tells you it is "in a (certain) life."

4.meaning: "pleasant / well-pleasing" — describing the life as satisfying and agreeable. The Arabic word actively means "pleasing," but classical commentators note a beautiful two-way sense: it is a life that pleases its owner, and a life he is fully pleased and content with — mutual satisfaction. It is the restful contentment of the people of Paradise.
4.grammar: An active participle (a describing word formed like "-ing," i.e. "pleasing") used as an adjective for ʿīshatin. The -a-…-i- shape (rāḍi-) is the active-participle pattern. The feminine -t and the indefinite genitive -in ending make it match the noun it describes — feminine, indefinite, and genitive — so it reads "a pleasing life." Arabic adjectives copy the case, gender, and definiteness of their noun, and this ending does exactly that.
4.root: ر-ض-و / ر-ض-ي (r-ḍ-w/y) — to be pleased, contentment, good pleasure

1.meaning: "But as for…" — this opens the second half of a two-sided contrast. The previous verses described the one whose good deeds weigh heavy; this word pivots to the opposite case, introducing the person whose scale comes up light. It functions like "now, on the other hand, as for the one who…", setting up a condition and the outcome that follows.

parts.en: and / but (connecting and contrasting with the previous verse)
as for / as regards (a particle that singles out a topic and demands a consequence)

1.grammar: Two pieces joined: wa- is the connector "and/but," and ammā is a detailing particle meaning "as for." It sets up a topic-and-result structure — "as for X … then Y" — where the matching "then" (fa-) lands on the verse's answer. There is no case ending here because these are particles, not nouns; they govern the clause rather than being governed by it.

2.meaning: "Whoever / the one who." It refers to any single human being who falls into this category — here, the person whose deeds turn out to weigh little. It is open-ended, covering anyone at all who fits the description, and acts as the subject that the rest of the sentence reports on.

parts.en: whoever / the one who (used for persons)

2.grammar: A relative/conditional noun meaning "whoever," used specifically for people (as opposed to mā, "whatever," for things). It carries a fixed shape with a silent ending (sukūn on the final n) and does not change for case. Grammatically it is the topic introduced by "as for," and the verb that follows describes it.

3.meaning: "Proved light / turned out to be light" — the deeds, when placed in the scale, weighed little and were found wanting. The verb conveys a completed result: at the reckoning, the measure of one's good came up short.

parts.en: she / it (feminine) — agreeing with the scales

3.grammar: A past-tense verb ("became light") that is third-person feminine SINGULAR. Its subject is "his scales" (mawāzīn), a broken plural of a non-human noun; in Arabic such plurals take feminine singular verb agreement, so the verb is singular, not plural. The literal sense is therefore "it [the set of scales] was light," i.e. his deeds weighed too little — not "they were light." The feminine marker is the tā' al-sākinah (تْ, a tā' carrying sukūn); the -a- sound heard before it belongs to the doubled-root stem خَفَّ (khaffa), so the full form is خَفَّتْ = khaffat.
3.root: خ-ف-ف (kh-f-f) — lightness, being light in weight

4.meaning: "His scales / the balances of his deeds." This is the set of scales in which a person's actions are weighed on the Day of Judgement; the attached "his" ties those scales to this particular individual. The plural form points to the weighing apparatus or the multiple weighings of one's deeds.

parts.en: scales / balances (plural of mīzān, a weighing-balance)
his / its (referring back to the person)

4.grammar: A plural noun "scales" with an attached possessive ending -hu, "his." The -u vowel before the ending is the nominative case, marking this word as the doer/subject of the verb — it is the thing that "became light." Because it is a broken plural of a non-human noun, it takes a feminine singular verb (khaffat). So the clause means "his scales became light," i.e. his deeds weighed too little.

1.meaning: "So his mother is..." — This word opens the verse's verdict on the person whose scale of good deeds is light. "Mother" (umm) is used figuratively: just as a mother is the one a child returns to and is sheltered by, this person's only refuge and final dwelling-place will be the Fire named in the next word. Some commentators instead take it of the head/brain, picturing him falling headfirst into the Fire; either way it names his ultimate abode and source of "shelter" — a bitterly ironic one.

parts.en: so / then (linking this to the previous verse)
mother (here: refuge, the place one returns to)

1.grammar: "fa-" is a connector meaning "so/then," tying this consequence to the preceding verse about the light scale. The core noun is umm ("mother"). Its ending is the -u of ummu, the nominative case, marking it as the subject (mubtadaʾ) of the sentence ("his mother IS..."). The attached "-hu" means "his" (3rd-person masculine singular possessive suffix); it is phonologically a short-vowel suffix (-hu), and the small superscript waw written over هٗ is a Quranic-script recitation convention indicating a slightly lengthened /u/, not a separate long-vowel morpheme. The whole is "so his mother..." — used metaphorically for one's final refuge.
1.root: أ-م-م (ʾ-m-m) — to head toward, to be a source/origin; hence umm (mother) and imām (one who leads)

2.meaning: A name of the Fire of Hell — literally "the one that plunges/falls" or "the Abyss/Pit." It pictures a bottomless chasm into which the doomed person tumbles, and at the same time the place that itself "falls" upon him. It is the predicate completing the previous word: his only refuge will be this plunging Pit.

parts.en: plunging one / the Abyss, the Pit (active participle, feminine)

2.grammar: This is an active participle (the "-er/-ing" form) from a verb meaning "to fall/plunge," so it means "the one that plunges" — either the falling person or the Pit that swallows him. The written ending -atun is made up of three distinct elements: -at, the tā' marbūta (ة), a fixed feminine morphological marker that is part of the word itself and present regardless of case or definiteness (here suiting its use as a name for the Fire); -u, the nominative case vowel; and -n, the tanwīn marking indefiniteness ("a"). Together they make it the indefinite nominative predicate: "his refuge is a plunging Abyss."
2.root: ه-و-ي (h-w-y) — to fall, plunge, drop down; hence hāwiya (an abyss/chasm)

1.meaning: "And what..." — the opening of a rhetorical question whose purpose is not to gather information but to magnify awe and dread. The 'and' links this verse to the warning before it, and the 'what' sets up the formula 'what could possibly make you grasp...?', implying the reality is beyond ordinary comprehension.
1.grammar: Two pieces joined together. 'wa-' is the connector 'and', tying this verse to what came before. 'mā' is an interrogative ('what?') used here for awe — it asks a question to overwhelm, not to be answered. It has no case ending of its own; the long final -ā is simply part of the fixed word, and the extra stretch (madd) reflects the dramatic recitation.

2.meaning: "...has made you realize / could ever let you know" — addressed to a single person (the Prophet, and through him every listener). The sense is: nothing in your experience can convey the true horror of this thing; only revelation can hint at it.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb (Form IV, the causative 'a-' pattern, from the root meaning 'to know'), so it means 'to MAKE someone know' rather than simply 'to know'. The ending '-ka' is an attached object pronoun: 'you' (one man). The verb's stem ends in a defective alif maqṣūra (the ٰى writing the root's final ى in Form IV), and the object pronoun '-ka' attaches directly to it. Verbs do not take case (iʿrāb) endings — case belongs to nouns and adjectives — so there is no case ending here at all; the long -ā is simply the verb's final stem vowel. Together: 'what has made you realize...'.
2.root: د-ر-ي (d-r-y) — to know, to be aware, to perceive

3.meaning: "...what..." — a second questioning word, this time introducing the actual thing being asked about: 'what IT is'. It turns the sentence into 'what could let you know WHAT it is?'
3.grammar: Again the interrogative 'mā' ('what'). Here it opens the small embedded question 'what is it?' that the verb 'made you realize' is pointing toward. It is a fixed, unchanging word with no case ending; the short final -ā is just part of the word.

4.meaning: "...it is" — 'it' refers back to al-Hāwiyah, the plunging abyss of Hellfire named in the previous verse. The whole line therefore reads: 'And what could ever make you realize what it (that abyss) is?' — leaving the answer to the next verse: 'a blazing fire'.

parts.en: a silent pause-letter (added at a stop)

4.grammar: The core word is 'hiya', the pronoun 'it/she' (Arabic treats 'the abyss/fire' as feminine, so 'she' = 'it'). The final 'هْ' is a hāʾ al-saktah — a 'pause hāʾ' carrying a sukūn (no vowel), added only to let the voice rest gently at the verse-end; it adds no meaning. Spelled out fully the word is hiyah, and it functions as the subject 'it' of the question 'what is it?'.

1.meaning: A fire — here the Fire of Hell itself, the dreadful reality of the Hawiyah (the abyss) named in the previous ayah. The word is left indefinite to convey awe and magnitude: 'a Fire' the like of which is beyond any ordinary fire.
1.grammar: A singular feminine noun. The final -un ending is tanwīn ḍamma (a single ḍamma vowel carrying the nunation -n), and it does two things at once: the 'u' vowel marks the nominative case (this word is the subject — the very thing being identified), and the -n nunation marks it as indefinite, so it means 'a Fire' rather than 'the Fire.' It stands as the answer to the question 'And what will make you know what it is?' from the preceding ayah.

2.meaning: Scorching, blazing, intensely hot — describing a fire heated to its utmost, raging and searing. It is an active participle (a 'doer' word) portraying the Fire as actively burning at full ferocity, not merely warm.
2.grammar: An active participle of the form fāʿil, here functioning as an adjective describing 'nār' (fire). Because the root ح-م-ي ends in the weak letter yāʾ, this is a defective participle with the underlying stem ḥāmiy-. The root-yāʾ is preserved in this feminine form (ḥāmiyah) because the following tāʾ marbūṭa shields it; in the masculine indefinite the same yāʾ elides before the tanwīn, giving ḥāmin. The -a(t)- is the feminine ending, matching 'nār,' which is grammatically feminine. The final -un is tanwīn ḍamma (a single ḍamma vowel carrying the nunation -n), marking the word nominative and indefinite in agreement with the noun it describes: 'a scorching Fire.' As a participle it conveys a vivid, ongoing sense — fire that is actively raging and searing.
2.root: ح-م-ي (ḥ-m-y) — to be intensely hot, to heat / blaze fiercely
